title: Understanding your pregnancy
overview: This guide goes with the “Understanding Your Pregnancy” section of your journal. It explains what is happening in your body, how to care for yourself day to day, and how to walk into every appointment informed and heard. Read each section before or after the matching journal page, whichever suits you.

stages.label: First trimester
stages.intro: The first trimester runs from the first day of your last period to the end of week 13. Your baby’s organs are forming, your hormones are rising quickly, and you may feel very different while looking exactly the same. This guide helps you make sense of how this pregnancy began, how to care for yourself, and how to get the most from your first appointments.

guides.title: My pregnancy, my story
guides.desc: Every pregnancy begins in its own way, and that beginning shapes how the first weeks feel. This guide explains why naming your story matters, why hope and worry so often arrive together in early pregnancy, and what is known about the fear of loss that many women carry quietly.

blocks.p: The first page of your journal asks how this pregnancy began, and how you are holding hope and worry. Most pregnancy resources assume a single story: planned, joyful, uncomplicated. Many women’s stories are different. A pregnancy may come as a surprise, after years of waiting, after fertility treatment, or after a loss. The way a pregnancy begins colours everything that follows, including how safe it feels to hope. Naming your own story gives your feelings a context, so they make sense rather than feeling like something is wrong with you.

ul: **If this pregnancy was planned or longed for,** you may feel joy alongside a fear of “jinxing” it, or pressure to feel only grateful.

**If it was unplanned,** you may feel shock, worry about timing, money, work, studies or spacing between children, or mixed feelings you don’t want anyone to see. Mixed feelings at the start are common and do not decide how you will feel about your baby later.

**After a long wait or fertility treatment,** a positive test may not bring the relief you expected. Many women describe staying on high alert, waiting for the next scan before they let themselves believe it.
**After a previous loss,** each twinge, cramp or day without nausea can feel like a warning. You may hold back from planning, buying anything, or telling people.

**Family and community** may add their own layer: questions about when you’ll “give good news”, advice to keep the pregnancy secret because of nazar, or comments about how soon this pregnancy came after the last one.

blocks.p: In the first trimester, your body is building the placenta and your baby’s organs are forming. Rising hormones such as hCG, progesterone and oestrogen support the pregnancy and also cause many early symptoms. Symptoms naturally come and go, and having fewer symptoms on some days is common. On its own, it does not tell you how the pregnancy is progressing.

Worry about miscarriage is the most common fear in early pregnancy, and it is not irrational. Miscarriage affects roughly 15 in every 100 recognised pregnancies, and most happen in the first trimester. Research shows that most early losses are caused by chromosomal differences in the pregnancy, not by anything the mother did: not work, lifting, travel, intercourse, spicy food or stress. Women who have experienced a loss before are more likely to feel anxious in a later pregnancy, and that anxiety is a recognised, understandable response, not a sign of weakness.

ul: **Circle everything that fits.** Many pregnancies begin with more than one of these at once, for example “a happy surprise” and “after a loss”.
**“What I’d like people to understand”** is for you first. You don’t have to share it. Writing it can help you notice what you need from others, such as patience, privacy or practical help.
**In “Holding hope and worry”,** name the worry as specifically as you can. “Something will go wrong” is hard to work with; “I’m scared the next scan will show no heartbeat” is easier to plan around.

**For “what steadies me”,** think of anything that has helped, even slightly: talking to your sister, a walk, prayer, a warm shower, getting clear information from your doctor, or a distraction that works.
**“Room for hope”** can be tiny: letting yourself imagine one ordinary moment with your baby, or saying “I’m pregnant today”.

blocks.p: You may notice that your worry gets louder at particular times: before scans, when symptoms change, at night, or after hearing someone else’s story. You may notice habits that bring brief relief but keep worry going, such as checking for symptoms many times a day or searching online for reassurance. You may also find that grief for an earlier loss sits alongside excitement for this pregnancy. Both can be true.

ul: **Plan for the hard moments.** If scans are your trigger, arrange for someone to come with you and plan something gentle afterwards.
**Put limits on checking.** If you find yourself searching or checking often, try setting one short time a day for it, and bring your questions to your next appointment instead (journal page 1.3).
**Choose who knows.** You decide when and with whom to share your news. Telling one trusted person early can mean you are not carrying the worry alone.
**Use your steadying list.** Keep what steadies you somewhere you can see it on hard days.

blocks.p: Writing about how this pregnancy began can bring up grief, guilt or old pain, especially after a loss, a difficult decision, or a long road through fertility treatment. Go slowly, and stop if you need to. If worry is present most of the day, keeps you from sleeping or eating, or turns into panic, you deserve support, and talking therapies are effective in pregnancy. If you are grieving a previous loss, it can help to talk with someone who understands pregnancy loss.

soon: Worry or low mood most of the day, on most days, for two weeks or more
Panic attacks, or being unable to sleep even when you have the chance
Spotting or light bleeding, so it can be checked
urgent: Heavy bleeding, or bleeding with cramping pain
Pain on one side of the lower abdomen, pain in the tip of the shoulder, or fainting (these can be signs of an ectopic pregnancy)

refs: Quenby, S., et al. (2021). Miscarriage matters: the epidemiology, physical, psychological, and economic costs of early pregnancy loss. The Lancet, 397(10285), 1658–1667.

Hunter, A., Tussis, L., & MacBeth, A. (2017). The presence of anxiety, depression and stress in women and their partners during pregnancies following perinatal loss: A meta-analysis. Journal of Affective Disorders, 223, 153–164.
Farren, J., et al. (2016). Post-traumatic stress, anxiety and depression following miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy: a prospective cohort study. BMJ Open, 6(11), e011864.
National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (2019, updated 2023). Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage: diagnosis and initial management (NG126).
World Health Organization (2016). WHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience.

guides.title: Caring for two
guides.desc: Caring for yourself in early pregnancy doesn’t mean following a perfect plan. This guide explains why folic acid, iron, fluids, rest and gentle movement matter now, how to work with nausea and tiredness instead of against them, and how a one-week plan helps small habits stick.

blocks.p: In early pregnancy, women are often given long lists of rules, from many directions at once. This page narrows that down to six foundations and one small plan for one week. The aim is not to do everything perfectly. It is to choose a few manageable actions, notice what works, and adjust.

ul: **Nausea and food aversions** can make eating well feel impossible some days. Smells from cooking, especially oil and spices, may be hard to bear.
**Deep tiredness** is common in the first trimester, often worse than you expected.

**Advice from every direction:** relatives may encourage you to “eat for two”, recommend desi ghee or certain foods as “garam” or “thanda”, or worry about what you’re eating. Some advice is helpful, and some conflicts with medical guidance.
**Guilt** if you can’t eat the way you planned, or can’t keep up with housework or work.

**Folic acid** taken before and in early pregnancy reduces the risk of neural tube defects, which affect the developing brain and spine. The neural tube forms in the first weeks, often before a woman knows she is pregnant, which is why it matters so much right now. The WHO recommends daily iron and folic acid supplements in pregnancy; your clinician can advise on the right product and dose for you.

**Iron** builds the extra blood your body needs in pregnancy. Iron-deficiency anaemia is common in pregnancy in Pakistan, and it adds to tiredness. Plant iron (daal, chickpeas, leafy greens) is absorbed better with vitamin C (lemon, guava, oranges), and less well with tea at the same meal.
**Fluids** matter more when you are nauseous or vomiting. Small, frequent sips are often easier than full glasses.
**Tiredness** in early pregnancy is driven by hormones, especially progesterone, and by the work of building the placenta. It usually eases in the second trimester.

**Movement:** for many uncomplicated pregnancies, guidelines suggest building towards about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, such as brisk walking, if your clinician agrees. Moving can ease tiredness, low mood and constipation.

**Food and medicine safety:** avoid alcohol, boil unpasteurised milk, cook meat and eggs thoroughly, and keep caffeine moderate (many guidelines suggest under 200 mg a day, about two mugs of instant coffee). Check any medicines, supplements or herbal and desi remedies with your clinician before taking them.
**Eating for two** is a myth in the first trimester. Your energy needs rise only modestly, mostly later in pregnancy. Quality matters more than quantity.

blocks.p: Big health goals often collapse when you are tired and nauseous. Research on behaviour change shows that specific, small plans tied to a particular moment (“After my morning chai, I’ll take my supplement”) are much more likely to be followed through than general intentions. The end-of-week review turns the plan into a gentle experiment: you are not passing or failing, you are learning what works for your body right now.

ul: **Choose one small action per line.** “Keep crackers by my bed” is a nourishing habit. “A 10-minute walk after Maghrib” is a movement plan. “Lie down for 20 minutes after lunch” is a rest plan.
**Make it fit your real day,** including family meals, work hours and prayer times.
**On days of bad nausea,** let fluids and anything you can keep down be enough.

blocks.p: At the end of the week, you may find that some things were easier than expected and others didn’t fit at all. You may notice patterns, like nausea being worse when you skip breakfast, or tiredness lifting a little after a short walk. You may also notice where family routines make your plan hard, which is useful to know.

Keep what worked, shrink what didn’t, and try again next week. If family meals make healthy choices hard, ask for one small change, such as a plain portion set aside before spices are added. Bring any questions about supplements, food or exercise to your next appointment (journal page 1.3).

If you can barely eat because of nausea, the goal this week is simply to stay hydrated and rest. That is enough. If thinking about food, weight or exercise makes you anxious, or you have a history of an eating disorder, please tell your clinician. Support during pregnancy makes a real difference.

soon: Vomiting most days, or struggling to eat for several days
Feeling unusually breathless, dizzy or exhausted (possible anaemia)
Cravings for non-food items such as clay, chalk or ice
urgent: Being unable to keep any fluids down for a day, very dark urine, or feeling faint

refs: World Health Organization (2016). WHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience.
De-Regil, L. M., et al. (2015). Effects and safety of periconceptional oral folate supplementation for preventing birth defects. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, CD007950.
American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (2020). Physical activity and exercise during pregnancy and the postpartum period. Committee Opinion No. 804.
Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (2016). The management of nausea and vomiting of pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum. Green-top Guideline No. 69.
Gollwitzer, P. M. (1999). Implementation intentions: Strong effects of simple plans. American Psychologist, 54(7), 493–503.

guides.title: My prenatal care plan
guides.desc: Your appointments are where questions get answered and decisions get made, but they are often short and easy to forget. This guide explains what early antenatal visits usually include, why writing things down helps, and how to make sure your voice is heard in your own care.

blocks.p: This page is the one place in your journal for appointments: your notes, your questions, and the people you can contact. Many women leave appointments with questions unasked, or unsure what was said. Preparing beforehand and writing things down afterwards helps you take part in decisions about your care rather than just receiving them.

ul: **Short appointments,** busy clinics, and long waits.
**Not knowing what to ask,** or feeling that your questions are too small to bother the doctor with.
**Someone else speaking for you,** such as a mother-in-law or husband, so your own questions go unasked.
**Unfamiliar medical words** and test names, sometimes in English when you think in Urdu or another language.
**Anxiety about tests and scans,** especially after a previous loss.

blocks.p: The WHO recommends at least eight antenatal contacts during pregnancy, with the first in the first trimester, ideally before 12 weeks. Early visits commonly include:

ul: Your medical history, previous pregnancies and family history
Blood pressure, weight and height
Blood tests, often including your blood group and Rh factor, haemoglobin for anaemia, and screening for infections such as hepatitis B and C, HIV and syphilis
A urine test
A dating scan to confirm the pregnancy, check the heartbeat, see whether there is more than one baby, and estimate your due date
A discussion of screening options for chromosomal conditions, which vary by hospital

blocks.p: Exact tests and timing depend on your health, your history and where you receive care.

Research on medical consultations shows that patients forget a large share of what they are told, and that anxiety makes this worse. Writing questions in advance and noting answers straight away are simple, effective ways to keep hold of information. Being prepared also changes how a consultation feels: it moves you from feeling passive to feeling like a partner in your care.

ul: **Fill in your appointment notes before you go,** including all medicines and supplements, and any herbal or desi remedies.
**Write the answers straight after the appointment,** while you remember them. A quiet moment in the waiting area or in the car works well.
**Add your own questions** at the bottom of the table. No question is too small.
**My support contacts:** write the name and number of your healthcare professional and your clinic or hospital, so they are easy to find in a hurry.
**Keep your reports** in one folder with this journal.

blocks.p: You may realise how many questions you have been carrying, or that some answers left you more confused. You may notice that you hold back when someone else is in the room. These are useful insights for your next visit.

ul: **Ask for clarity:** “Could you explain that in simpler words?” or “Can you write that down for me?”
**Check your understanding:** repeat back what you heard: “So I should take this once a day, with food?”
**Ask for privacy if you need it:** you can ask to speak to the doctor alone for part of the visit.
**Ask for a female doctor** if that matters to you.
**Bring someone supportive** who will help you remember and ask, not speak over you.

blocks.p: If hospitals or examinations bring back difficult memories, or a previous pregnancy ended in loss, appointments can feel frightening. Tell your clinician; it helps them care for you. If you have had a bad experience with care before, you are allowed to ask questions, ask for explanations, and ask for a second opinion.

soon: Burning or pain when passing urine
Spotting, or any bleeding, so it can be checked
Vomiting that stops you eating most of the day
urgent: Heavy bleeding, or bleeding with severe pain
Severe abdominal or pelvic pain, especially on one side, or pain in the tip of the shoulder
Fainting, or severe or rapidly worsening symptoms

refs: World Health Organization (2016). WHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience.
National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (2021). Antenatal care (NG201).
Kessels, R. P. C. (2003). Patients’ memory for medical information. Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine, 96(5), 219–222.

title: Your body and confidence
overview: This guide goes with the “Your Body and Confidence” section of your journal. It explains the thinking behind each exercise, what you may be going through, and how to use what you discover with more understanding and less self-criticism. You don’t have to love every change to use it. Honest is enough.

stages.label: First trimester
stages.intro: In the first trimester, the biggest changes are felt rather than seen. Many women feel unwell and unlike themselves while looking exactly the same, often while keeping the pregnancy private. This guide helps you make sense of that inside-out experience, and of the beliefs about bodies you bring into pregnancy.

guides.title: The quiet signals
guides.desc: In early pregnancy your body speaks in sensations before it shows any change. This guide explains how to notice those signals, why separating a sensation from the meaning your mind gives it can ease distress, and how to use the symbol key and silhouette on your page.

blocks.p: In early pregnancy your body speaks mainly in sensations. This exercise helps you notice those signals, and separate the sensation itself from the meaning your mind gives it.

Rising pregnancy hormones are linked with nausea, tiredness, breast tenderness, bloating and needing to urinate more often. Because nothing shows yet, you may feel you have to carry on as normal, which can make symptoms feel more isolating. Some sensations, such as cramping, may also trigger fear about the pregnancy.

Our awareness of internal bodily signals, called interoception, is closely tied to how we experience emotion. Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) adds a useful distinction: a sensation is one thing, and our interpretation of it is another. The same nausea can be read as “my body is failing me” or “this is hard, and it’s temporary”, and each reading brings a different feeling. Research on emotion also shows that simply putting a feeling into words can soften its intensity.

ul: **Mark the silhouette** using the six symbols beside it, without trying to fix anything. This page is about listening, not solving.
**Include the heart symbol** if anything feels okay, even small things like warm hands or a good night’s sleep.
**In the table, write the first thought that comes** in “What goes through my mind”, not the sensible one. That raw thought is what you are looking for.
**If you’re not sure how a sensation makes you feel,** try words like annoyed, worried, tired of it, curious or okay.

**The three lines at the bottom** (what affects my mood most, what I tend to think on those days, and something that helps) are about patterns. If a pattern isn’t clear yet, come back to them after a few days.

blocks.p: Some signals carry more emotional weight than others because of what they mean to you. A cramp may matter far more than nausea if you have experienced loss before. You may find your mind adds blame (“I’m weak”) or alarm (“something’s wrong”) to ordinary sensations. You may also find the heart symbol surprisingly hard to place.

Try saying the sensation and the story separately: “I feel nauseous. My mind is telling me I’m useless.” This small gap often reduces the sting. Your marked silhouette can also help you explain invisible tiredness to your husband or family. Use the last three prompts to collect comforts that work, however small.

If focusing on your body makes you more anxious, especially after a previous loss, keep this brief and turn your attention outward afterwards, to a task, a person or sounds around you. This page is for emotional awareness, not for checking symptoms. Bleeding, severe pain or being unable to keep fluids down need your doctor, not this page.

refs: Farb, N., et al. (2015). Interoception, contemplative practice, and health. Frontiers in Psychology, 6, 763.
Beck, J. S. (2011). Cognitive behavior therapy: Basics and beyond (2nd ed.). Guilford Press.
Lieberman, M. D., et al. (2007). Putting feelings into words: Affect labeling disrupts amygdala activity in response to affective stimuli. Psychological Science, 18(5), 421–428.

guides.title: What I imagined, what arrived
guides.desc: Most women carry a picture of early pregnancy that reality doesn’t match. This guide explains why that gap so often turns into guilt, what “should statements” are, and how to rewrite them in a way that is truer and kinder rather than falsely positive.

blocks.p: Most women carry a mental picture of early pregnancy, often a glowing, joyful one. When reality looks different, the gap can turn into guilt. This exercise brings the gap into the open and loosens the rules that make you feel you are falling short.

Instead of a glow, you may have nausea, exhaustion, breakouts and no sense of connection to the baby yet. You may feel you have no right to complain, especially if others around you have struggled to conceive, or if you are told repeatedly to be grateful.

CBT calls rigid inner rules “should statements”. They feel like facts but are really expectations, and when we break them, guilt and shame follow. Cognitive restructuring does not replace a should with forced positivity. It asks where the rule came from, whether it is fair, and what a more accurate statement would be. Starting your rewrite with “Right now, it makes sense that I…” builds in validation, which is often what a harsh should is missing.

ul: **In the two columns,** write a few things you imagined these weeks would feel like on the left, and what actually arrived on the right. Be specific, including small details.
**When circling shoulds,** notice the tone they have in your head. Whose voice is it?
**Before you rewrite,** ask yourself one question: is this rule fair, given everything your body is doing right now?
**Aim for true rather than cheerful.** For example: “Right now, it makes sense that I’m not glowing. My body is using a huge amount of energy.”

blocks.p: Some shoulds may come from family, dramas or social media; others may be your own high standards. You may notice the gap holds grief for the pregnancy you imagined. You might also find some things are better than you expected.

Copy your rewritten statement somewhere you’ll see it. If a should is shaping your days, such as “I should manage the house like before”, it may need a practical change as well as a new thought, like asking for help with heavy tasks.

If you feel guilty for admitting the gap, remember that naming difficulty doesn’t cancel gratitude; both can be true (see 1.4 below). If the gap feels mostly like emptiness or hopelessness that lasts two weeks or more, talk to your doctor.

refs: Burns, D. D. (1980). Feeling good: The new mood therapy. William Morrow.
Beck, J. S. (2011). Cognitive behavior therapy: Basics and beyond (2nd ed.). Guilford Press.

guides.title: The voices I inherited
guides.desc: You came into pregnancy with years of messages about what a woman’s body should be, and those messages tend to get louder as your body changes. This guide explains where those voices come from, why separating yourself from them helps, and what “return to sender” really means.

blocks.p: You came into pregnancy with years of messages about what a woman’s body should be. As your body changes, those messages tend to get louder. This exercise identifies them early, so you can choose which to keep.

In many Pakistani families, girls hear frequent comments about weight, skin colour, height and hair, sometimes linked to marriage prospects. Modesty teachings may be meaningful to you, and may also have left a sense that the body is something to hide or feel uneasy about. Other messages may be warm and protective. Most women carry a mix.

Narrative therapy suggests that many problems come from stories we absorbed from our families and culture, which then feel like truths about ourselves. “Externalising” separates you from the message: the message is “your skin is too dark”, not “I am too dark”. Objectification theory describes how repeated attention to women’s appearance teaches women to monitor themselves from the outside. Women with a more positive body image tend to filter such messages, letting in helpful ones and screening out harmful ones. “Return to sender” is a written version of that filtering.

ul: **Answer only what you can.** There’s no need to fill every line.
**When you think about what a “good” body meant where you grew up,** consider skin colour, size, hair, modesty and how a woman was expected to carry herself.
**For “Whose voice is it?”,** write a person, or a source such as school, dramas, social media or the wider family.
**A voice can be loving and still carry a harmful message.** You can love your aunt and return her comment.
**“Keep” is for messages that genuinely help you,** such as a grandmother who praised your strong hands.
**“Return to sender” simply means:** this was never really mine to carry, and I don’t have to take it with me into motherhood.
**“Not sure yet” is a real answer.** Some messages need time. You can come back and move them later.

blocks.p: You may find that many critical messages were never yours, and that the same comments have passed down through generations of women in your family. Some may tie a woman’s worth to how she looks.

As your pregnancy becomes visible, comments about your body often increase. When one lands hard, check whether it echoes one of these old voices. Your message for your child can guide how you speak about your own body in front of them, which is one of the ways children learn about bodies.

This exercise can stir painful memories of teasing, bullying or worse. Stop when you need to and do something grounding. You don’t need to confront anyone. If memories of abuse or severe shame come up, a counsellor or psychologist can help you work through them safely.

refs: White, M., & Epston, D. (1990). Narrative means to therapeutic ends. W. W. Norton.
Fredrickson, B. L., & Roberts, T.-A. (1997). Objectification theory. Psychology of Women Quarterly, 21(2), 173–206.
Wood-Barcalow, N. L., Tylka, T. L., & Augustus-Horvath, C. L. (2010). “But I like my body”: Positive body image characteristics and a holistic model for young-adult women. Body Image, 7(2), 106–116.

guides.title: Both are true
guides.desc: Early pregnancy often brings feelings that seem to contradict each other. This guide explains why trying to push the uncomfortable half away tends to backfire, and how the small switch from “but” to “and” lets both feelings be real.

blocks.p: Early pregnancy often brings feelings that seem to contradict each other. Many women feel they must choose, or hide the uncomfortable half. This exercise practises holding both.

Excitement and dread, love and resentment of how unwell you feel, hope and fear of loss, gratitude and grief for your old body and freedom. If the pregnancy was unplanned, or follows a loss, these mixtures can be stronger.

Acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) teaches that struggling to push feelings away often makes them stronger, and that we can make room for difficult feelings while still acting on what matters. The small switch from “but” to “and” reflects this. “I feel sick, but I’m grateful” quietly cancels the first half; “I feel sick, and I’m grateful” lets both be real.

ul: **Start with the hard feeling,** honestly.
**The part after “and” doesn’t have to be positive.** It can be a fact (“and it usually eases”), a value (“and I want to look after myself”), or a permission (“and that’s allowed”).
**Two more examples,** beyond the ones on the page: “I’m scared something might go wrong, and I’m allowed to hope.” “I miss how my body used to feel, and I chose this.”

blocks.p: You may notice which feelings you have been pushing away. Your “and” statements often point towards what matters to you.
Choose one statement to repeat on hard days, perhaps written on your phone lock screen or said quietly during a wave of nausea.

If nothing comes after “and”, write “I feel ___, and I don’t know what else yet.” That is honest and enough. If you have lost a pregnancy before, holding back from feeling attached is a common, protective response; you don’t have to force hope.

refs: Hayes, S. C., Strosahl, K. D., & Wilson, K. G. (2012). Acceptance and commitment therapy: The process and practice of mindful change (2nd ed.). Guilford Press.

guides.title: A little note to the body working in secret
guides.page: A little note to the body working in secret
guides.desc: You don’t have to love your body to write to it. This guide explains why an honest note to your body can be helpful, the difference between respecting your body and liking how it looks, and how small acts of care can shift how you feel.

blocks.p: This short note starts a different kind of relationship with your body, based on honesty and respect rather than love or blame. Keep it: reading it again later in pregnancy, or after your baby arrives, can show you how far you have come.
You may feel frustrated with your body, distant from it, or quietly amazed by it. Many women feel all three in a single week. Your body has been doing a great deal without anyone noticing.

Expressive writing about emotional experiences has been linked with benefits to wellbeing in many studies. The note also draws on self-compassion, which includes kindness towards yourself, recognising that struggle is part of being human, and noticing pain without being swept away by it. Higher self-compassion is associated with lower anxiety and depression. Positive body image research separates respecting and caring for your body from liking how it looks, which is why the journal says “respect is enough; love is optional”. The final prompt connects feelings to small acts of care.

ul: **Choose the opening that is most true today,** not most pleasant.
**Be specific** about what you notice your body doing.
**Keep what you’ll “give” realistic:** one or two things you can really manage, like one glass of water or one early night.

blocks.p: You may find more anger than you expected, or more tenderness. You might realise how much you have asked of your body without acknowledging it.
Pick one item from your “give” list and do it this week. Notice whether caring for your body changes how you feel about it, even slightly.

If writing to your body feels strange, write to yourself instead. If anger comes out, let it; it is a real part of your experience. If your body carries a history of illness, pain or harm, this can feel complicated, and keeping the note short is fine.

refs: Pennebaker, J. W. (1997). Writing about emotional experiences as a therapeutic process. Psychological Science, 8(3), 162–166.
Neff, K. D. (2003). Self-compassion: An alternative conceptualization of a healthy attitude toward oneself. Self and Identity, 2(2), 85–101.
MacBeth, A., & Gumley, A. (2012). Exploring compassion: A meta-analysis of the association between self-compassion and psychopathology. Clinical Psychology Review, 32(6), 545–552.
Tylka, T. L., & Wood-Barcalow, N. L. (2015). What is and what is not positive body image? Body Image, 14, 118–129.

title: Mental and emotional wellbeing
overview: This guide goes with the “Mental and Emotional Wellbeing” section of your journal. It explains why pregnancy can bring such strong and changeable feelings, how to work with worried thoughts without dismissing real concerns, and how to build steadiness and self-kindness. It also explains clearly when it’s time to reach out for more support.

stages.label: First trimester
stages.intro: The first trimester can bring a whole sky of feelings: joy, worry, irritability, numbness, sometimes all in one day. Hormones, nausea, tiredness and big life changes all play a part. This guide helps you name what you feel, look closely at worried thoughts, and respond to yourself with more kindness.

guides.title: Understanding my emotional world
guides.desc: Naming a feeling is the first step to understanding what it needs. This guide explains why emotions can feel so strong and changeable in early pregnancy, how putting feelings into words helps, and how to turn a feeling into a clue about what you need.

blocks.p: Many women feel emotions more strongly in early pregnancy but don’t always know what they are feeling, or why. This page asks you to name your feelings, notice what was happening when they appeared, and wonder what they might be telling you. It’s a way to turn a fog of emotion into information you can use.

ul: **Mood swings:** laughing one moment, crying the next.
**Irritability,** often directed at the people closest to you, and guilt afterwards.
**Worry** about the baby, the pregnancy, money, work or how your life will change.
**Mixed or unexpected feelings,** such as feeling flat, ambivalent or not yet connected to the pregnancy.
**Loneliness,** especially if you have moved away from your own family after marriage, or are keeping the pregnancy private.

blocks.p: In early pregnancy, oestrogen and progesterone rise rapidly, and these hormones influence brain chemicals involved in mood. Nausea, tiredness and broken sleep lower your capacity to cope with ordinary stress. Life changes, relationships and practical worries add their own weight. Feeling more emotional is a common, understandable response to all of this.

For some women, feelings go beyond ordinary ups and downs. Studies in low- and middle-income countries, including Pakistan, have found that roughly one in six women experience depression or anxiety during pregnancy. These are common, treatable conditions, not personal failures.

Research shows that simply putting a feeling into words can reduce its intensity. Emotions also carry information: anger may signal a boundary being crossed, sadness may signal loss, anxiety may signal uncertainty or threat, and loneliness may signal a need for connection. Asking “What might this feeling be telling me I need?” turns a feeling from something to get rid of into a signal worth listening to.

ul: **Circle as many words as fit.** More than one feeling at once is normal.
**Use “Something else” for feelings not on the list.** Common ones in early pregnancy include ambivalent, scared, numb, guilty, unready, relieved or jealous.
**For “What was happening”,** think about the moment: who was there, what had just happened, whether you were tired or hungry.
**For “What might this feeling be telling me I need”,** try finishing: “I think I need more…” or “I think I need less…”
**For “My emotional weather”,** you don’t need any drawing skill. Clouds, rain, sunshine, a storm, fog or a rainbow all work. Colours and scribbles are fine too.

blocks.p: You may notice patterns: feelings that come at a particular time of day, around certain people, or when you’re hungry or exhausted. You may notice that some feelings, like anger or jealousy, feel less acceptable to you, and that you push them away. You may also find that a need, such as rest, help or reassurance, sits underneath a feeling that looked like something else.

ul: **Try a daily pause.** Once a day, ask yourself three questions: What am I feeling? What may have led to it? What do I need right now?
**Act on one need.** If the feeling points to rest, help or company, try to meet that need in one small way today.
**Share a feeling with someone you trust.** Saying “I’ve been feeling irritable and I think I’m exhausted” helps people understand you.

blocks.p: It’s fine if you can’t name what you feel; “I don’t know” is a valid answer. If you feel numb, empty, hopeless or anxious most of the day, on most days, for two weeks or more, that may be more than ordinary pregnancy mood, and support can help. You don’t need to wait until things are unbearable to talk to someone.

soon: Low mood, emptiness or loss of interest most days for two weeks or more
Constant worry or panic that affects sleep, eating or daily life
Feeling disconnected from yourself or from the pregnancy for weeks
urgent: Thoughts of harming yourself, or feeling that others would be better off without you

refs: Lieberman, M. D., et al. (2007). Putting feelings into words: Affect labeling disrupts amygdala activity in response to affective stimuli. Psychological Science, 18(5), 421–428.

Fisher, J., et al. (2012). Prevalence and determinants of common perinatal mental disorders in women in low- and lower-middle-income countries: a systematic review. Bulletin of the World Health Organization, 90(2), 139–149G.
National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (2014, updated 2020). Antenatal and postnatal mental health: Clinical management and service guidance (CG192).

guides.title: When thoughts feel overwhelming
guides.desc: Worried thoughts can feel like facts, especially in early pregnancy. This guide explains how the thought detective works, walks through a full example, and shows how to look at a worry closely without dismissing a real concern.

blocks.p: Pregnancy brings many “what ifs”. Some worries are useful, prompting you to ask a question or take a step. Others grow and repeat until they feel like facts. This page helps you slow a thought down, look at it carefully, and decide what to do with it, rather than being carried along by it.

ul: **What-if spirals** about miscarriage, scans, the baby’s health, birth, money or how you’ll cope.
**Night-time worry** that feels much bigger at 3 a.m. than in daylight.
**Searching online** for reassurance and finding the most frightening stories instead.
**Worry passed on by others,** such as relatives’ stories of difficult births or losses.

blocks.p: In CBT, thoughts that pop up automatically in response to a situation are called “automatic thoughts”. They often follow familiar patterns, such as jumping to the worst outcome or treating a feeling as proof (“I feel scared, so something must be wrong”). A thought record slows this down: you write down the situation, the thought, the feeling and the evidence, and then look for a more balanced view and a helpful next step.

Two other ideas on the page come from acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT). The “influence” circle separates what you can act on from what you can’t control, so energy goes where it can help. “Unhooking” means noticing a thought as a thought (“I’m having the thought that…”) instead of arguing with it or obeying it.

ol: **The situation:** I noticed I didn’t feel sick this morning.
**My automatic thought:** Something has gone wrong with the pregnancy.
**Evidence:** For: I’ve heard that losing symptoms can be a bad sign. Against: symptoms often come and go in early pregnancy, I felt sick last night, and I have no pain or bleeding.
**A more balanced thought:** Symptoms change from day to day, and on their own they don’t show how the pregnancy is doing. I can ask my doctor about this at my next visit.
**One helpful next step:** Write this question in my appointment notes, and call my sister instead of searching online.

blocks.p: Notice that the balanced thought is not “nothing will ever go wrong”. It is more accurate, and it leads to an action.

ul: **Choose one specific thought,** not a general worry.
**Write the thought exactly as it sounds in your head.**
**For health worries, keep evidence simple and honest,** and let your clinician provide the medical facts. The thought detective is not a way to diagnose yourself.
**Aim for balanced, not positive.** A good balanced thought sounds believable to you.

blocks.p: You may notice that certain kinds of thoughts recur, such as worst-case predictions or self-blame. You may see that the feeling arrived before the evidence. You may find that your “next step” is often to ask a question, talk to someone, or rest.

ul: **Take one action within your influence each time,** however small.
**Keep a short list of your most common thought patterns,** so you can recognise them faster: “That’s my worst-case thought again.”
**Practise unhooking** when you can’t do a full thought record, such as at night or during a busy day.

blocks.p: A thought record can be demanding when you’re tired and nauseous; doing one or two steps is fine. Some women experience sudden, unwanted thoughts or images, for example of harm coming to the baby. These intrusive thoughts are common in pregnancy and early parenthood, are not wishes or intentions, and tend to become more frequent when we fight them. If they are frequent and distressing, or lead to lots of checking or avoiding, a professional can help.

soon: Worry that takes up much of your day, or that you can’t switch off
Intrusive thoughts that are frequent or very distressing
Checking, searching or seeking reassurance many times a day

refs: Beck, J. S. (2011). Cognitive behavior therapy: Basics and beyond (2nd ed.). Guilford Press.
Hayes, S. C., Strosahl, K. D., & Wilson, K. G. (2012). Acceptance and commitment therapy: The process and practice of mindful change (2nd ed.). Guilford Press.
Dennis, C.-L., Falah-Hassani, K., & Shiri, R. (2017). Prevalence of antenatal and postnatal anxiety: systematic review and meta-analysis. British Journal of Psychiatry, 210(5), 315–323.

guides.title: Building resilience and self-compassion
guides.desc: Resilience isn’t never struggling; it’s finding your way back. This guide explains how self-compassion works, why it isn’t the same as being easy on yourself, how values give direction when things feel hard, and what a simple support plan can do.

blocks.p: Many women in Pakistan are taught to be strong, patient and selfless, to have sabr and keep going. Those qualities can be real strengths. But when strength means never resting, never asking, and speaking harshly to yourself, it wears you down. This page offers three tools: a self-compassion pause for hard moments, your values for direction, and a support plan for when things feel like too much.

ul: **A harsh inner voice:** “You’re being dramatic.” “Other women manage, why can’t you?”
**Caring for everyone else first,** and leaving yourself until last, or not at all.
**Feeling you have to be strong** in front of family, and having nowhere to put your own feelings.

blocks.p: Self-compassion, as described by researcher Kristin Neff, has three parts: noticing that you are struggling, recognising that struggle is part of being human, and responding to yourself with kindness. It is not self-pity or lowering your standards. Research consistently links higher self-compassion with lower anxiety and depression. The question “What would I say to someone I love?” works because most of us are far kinder to others than to ourselves.

Values, in acceptance and commitment therapy, are directions rather than goals: you never finish being kind or honest, but you can take a step in that direction today. Values help on hard days because they give meaning to effort.

Support matters too. In Pakistan, the Thinking Healthy programme, delivered by Lady Health Workers, helped mothers with depression recover by combining simple psychological tools with practical support and involving the family.

ul: **The self-compassion pause:** answer the three questions in order. If kind words are hard to find, try “This is really hard right now”, “Many mothers feel this way”, or “What do I need?”
**Values:** circle two or three that feel most true, not the ones you think you should choose.
**One small action:** choose something you could do in ten minutes, such as calling a friend (connection), resting without guilt (health), or praying quietly (faith).

**Your support plan:** for “When I feel overwhelmed, I can”, list two or three things that genuinely help you, such as stepping outside, slow breathing, talking to someone, or making wudu and praying. For “A professional I can contact”, write a name and number: your gynaecologist, Lady Health Visitor, GP, or a psychologist.
**For the people around you,** use the support circle on the postpartum support plan page (Preparing for childbirth and motherhood, 1.2).

blocks.p: Kind words to yourself may feel awkward or untrue at first. You may notice that your inner critic speaks in a familiar voice. You may find that a value you hold dear, like family, has been crowding out another, like health.

Use the self-compassion pause whenever you catch the harsh voice. Keep your support plan somewhere you can find it quickly, and share it with someone you trust. Revisit your values when you have a decision to make.

Some people find self-compassion uncomfortable, especially if they grew up with criticism. This is common and gets easier with practice. If you feel you don’t deserve kindness, or feel hopeless, please talk to someone. A professional can help you with those feelings.

soon: Feeling hopeless, worthless or guilty most of the time
Being unable to cope with daily life
urgent: Thoughts of harming yourself, or feeling your family would be better off without you

refs: Neff, K. D. (2003). Self-compassion: An alternative conceptualization of a healthy attitude toward oneself. Self and Identity, 2(2), 85–101.
MacBeth, A., & Gumley, A. (2012). Exploring compassion: A meta-analysis of the association between self-compassion and psychopathology. Clinical Psychology Review, 32(6), 545–552.
Gilbert, P. (2009). The compassionate mind. Constable.
Hayes, S. C., Strosahl, K. D., & Wilson, K. G. (2012). Acceptance and commitment therapy: The process and practice of mindful change (2nd ed.). Guilford Press.

Rahman, A., et al. (2008). Cognitive behaviour therapy-based intervention by community health workers for mothers with depression and their infants in rural Pakistan: a cluster-randomised controlled trial. The Lancet, 372(9642), 902–909.

title: Preparing for childbirth and motherhood
overview: This guide goes with the “Preparing for Childbirth and Motherhood” section of your journal. It helps you learn about birth without fear-mongering, plan the support you’ll need after your baby arrives, and reflect on the mother you are becoming. There is no rush: in the first trimester, this is about learning and noticing, not deciding everything.

stages.label: First trimester
stages.intro: It may feel early to think about birth and motherhood. But a little gentle preparation now, such as learning your options, noticing who could support you and reflecting on the mother you hope to be, can make the months ahead feel calmer and more your own.

guides.title: Getting ready for birth
guides.desc: You don’t need a birth plan in the first trimester, but learning your options early can ease fear and help you ask better questions later. This guide explains what birth preferences are, what to find out about where you’ll give birth, and why feeling respected matters as much as any plan.

blocks.p: Many women first hear about birth through frightening stories from relatives, friends or dramas. This page replaces some of that fear with information and questions. It isn’t asking you to decide anything yet. It is asking you to start learning, so that by the third trimester your choices feel informed and your own.

ul: **Fear of pain,** of something going wrong, or of losing control.
**Uncertainty about where you’ll give birth,** and what that hospital or clinic allows.
**Pressure or assumptions about how you’ll give birth,** for example that a caesarean is easier, or that a vaginal birth is the only “real” birth.
**Worry about privacy and respect:** who will examine you, and whether you’ll be covered and kept informed.

**Birth preferences** are a flexible record of what matters to you. Birth can unfold differently from what you imagine, and your care team can help you make decisions as circumstances change. A plan works best as a conversation starter, not a contract.
**Where:** facilities differ widely in Pakistan. Some hospitals offer epidurals at all hours; some don’t. Some allow a companion in the labour room; many limit who can come in.

**Who:** the WHO recommends that every woman has a companion of her choice during labour. Research shows that continuous support during labour is linked with better birth experiences and outcomes, including women feeling more satisfied and needing less pain relief.

**Respect:** the WHO also recommends respectful maternity care: privacy, clear explanation, consent before procedures and kind communication. Research worldwide has documented births where this was missing, which is why asking about it in advance matters.

**Birth possibilities:** vaginal birth, assisted birth (using forceps or a vacuum cup) and caesarean birth are all ways babies are born. None is a personal success or failure. Each may be the right choice in different circumstances.
**Read the four tiles as a learning list.** Over the coming months, try to find out the answer to each one for your own hospital.
**Tick the appointment questions as you ask them,** and write the answers in your prenatal care notes (Understanding your pregnancy, 1.3).

**For “What would help me feel safe and respected”,** think about the details that matter to you: a female doctor, being told before any examination, being kept covered, having your mother or husband nearby.
**For “The person I’d like to support me”,** think about who keeps you calm, not only who is expected to come.

blocks.p: You may realise that some fears come from stories rather than facts. You may find that what matters most to you is not a particular type of birth but feeling informed, respected and supported. You may also notice gaps, such as not knowing which hospital you’ll use, that are worth sorting out early.

ul: **Talk about your preferences with your husband and family early,** especially around who will be with you and which hospital you’ll use.
**Visit the hospital, if you can,** later in pregnancy.
**Come back to this page in the third trimester,** when you’re ready to make a fuller plan.

blocks.p: Thinking about birth can bring up intense fear for some women. A severe fear of childbirth is recognised and treatable, and support early in pregnancy helps. If you’ve had a frightening birth before, ask your doctor to go through what happened and how this time could be different.

soon: Fear of birth that affects your sleep, mood or daily life
A previous birth that still causes distress, flashbacks or nightmares

refs: World Health Organization (2018). WHO recommendations: Intrapartum care for a positive childbirth experience.
Bohren, M. A., et al. (2017). Continuous support for women during childbirth. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, CD003766.
Bohren, M. A., et al. (2015). The mistreatment of women during childbirth in health facilities globally: A mixed-methods systematic review. PLOS Medicine, 12(6), e1001847.

guides.title: Building my postpartum support plan
guides.desc: The weeks after birth are a major physical and emotional transition. This guide explains why support is one of the strongest protections for a new mother’s wellbeing, how to make each item on the checklist practical, and which signs after birth need urgent care.

blocks.p: Most planning in pregnancy focuses on the birth day. But the weeks that follow, when you are healing, feeding and learning to care for a newborn, are often harder. This page helps you plan support now, while you have the energy to think clearly, rather than in the exhausted first days.

ul: **Uncertainty about where you’ll stay** after birth, at your mother’s home or your in-laws’, and for how long.
**Expectations around chilla,** the 40-day rest period, which can be a real source of care and also bring rules you may not agree with.
**Worry about visitors,** housework, or your husband’s work schedule.
**Reluctance to ask for help,** or not wanting to seem demanding.

blocks.p: Research consistently finds that lack of social support is one of the strongest risk factors for postnatal depression. Practical help, such as meals, sleep and someone to hold the baby, and emotional support, someone who listens without judging, both protect your wellbeing. The WHO recommends several postnatal check-ups in the first six weeks, for both you and your baby, starting within the first day after birth.

ul: **Be specific.** “Can you cook dinner on the days I’m alone?” is much easier to say yes to than “Please help me.”
**Healthcare contact:** write down who will check on you after birth, whether that’s your gynaecologist, a hospital clinic or a Lady Health Visitor.
**Physical changes:** ask your clinician what to expect after birth, such as bleeding for several weeks, and which signs need urgent care (listed below).
**Feeding:** find out where you can get skilled, non-judgemental feeding support, such as a lactation consultant, a trained nurse or an experienced LHV.
**Recovery space:** a comfortable spot to rest and feed, with water, snacks and pads within reach.
**Visitors and boundaries:** agree in advance who will manage visitors and how long visits last. A husband or mother saying “She needs to rest now” is often easier than you saying it.
**Sleep:** plan who can take a few night hours so you can get one longer stretch of sleep.

**Your support circle** works best with different people for different needs: someone you can call for practical help, someone you can talk to honestly, and one task you’d like others to take off your plate.

blocks.p: You may realise that support is concentrated on one or two people, or that you have more people around you than you thought. You may notice that it’s easier to accept practical help than emotional help, or the reverse.
Share your plan with your husband and the people involved, ideally before the third trimester. Write down the one task you most want taken off your plate, and ask for it directly.

If your husband works away, you live far from your family, or relationships at home are strained, planning support can bring up sadness or worry. Consider paid help for one heavy task, a neighbour or friend for meals, and regular video calls with family. Ask your doctor or LHV about home visits.

urgent: Heavy bleeding after birth, such as soaking a pad in an hour or passing large clots
A severe headache or changes in vision
Pain, redness or swelling in one leg
Thoughts of harming yourself or your baby

refs: Robertson, E., Grace, S., Wallington, T., & Stewart, D. E. (2004). Antenatal risk factors for postpartum depression: a synthesis of recent literature. General Hospital Psychiatry, 26(4), 289–295.
World Health Organization (2022). WHO recommendations on maternal and newborn care for a positive postnatal experience.
Rahman, A., et al. (2008). Cognitive behaviour therapy-based intervention by community health workers for mothers with depression and their infants in rural Pakistan. The Lancet, 372(9642), 902–909.

guides.title: Meeting the mother I am becoming
guides.page: Meeting the mother I am becoming
guides.desc: Becoming a mother is a change in identity as well as in daily life. This guide explains why imagining yourself as a mother is useful, how the mothers who raised you shape the mother you’ll be, and why you can choose what to carry forward.

blocks.p: Pregnancy is not only preparation for a baby; it is the start of becoming a mother. This page invites you to picture that change, to notice your hopes and fears about it, and to reflect on the women who mothered you. Doing this early, gently, gives you more choice about the kind of mother you become.

ul: **Excitement and fear** at the same time.
**Doubt:** “Will I know what to do?” “Will I be good at this?”
**Expectations from others** about what a good mother does and doesn’t do.
**Memories of your own childhood,** both warm and painful, appearing unexpectedly.

blocks.p: Psychiatrist Daniel Stern described becoming a mother as a deep reorganisation of identity, in which a woman’s focus, relationships and sense of self shift around caring for a child. Others have called this transition matrescence.

How we were cared for as children shapes how we care for our own children, often without our noticing. Child psychologists describe painful patterns that repeat unseen as “ghosts in the nursery”. More recent research describes “angels in the nursery”: memories of being loved and cared for, which protect and guide new parents. Reflecting on both gives you more choice about what to repeat and what to change.

ul: **For “When I imagine myself as a mother”,** picture a specific scene, such as feeding your baby at night or walking with your child, and describe what you see.
**Name both excitement and fear honestly.** Neither one predicts what kind of mother you will be.
**For “The mothers who shaped me”,** include anyone who mothered you: your mother, nani, dadi, an aunt, an older sister, a teacher.
**For “carry forward”,** think of small things as well as big ones: a song, a way of comforting, a phrase that made you feel loved.
**For “do differently”,** be honest but kind, to them and to yourself. Most people did what they could with what they had.
**For the expectation to release,** choose one that feels heavy, such as “I must never need help” or “I must know what to do immediately”.

blocks.p: You may find that your fears are mostly about not knowing yet, which is normal before any new role. You may discover warm memories you had forgotten. You may also notice patterns you don’t want to repeat, and that naming them already loosens their grip.

Share one “carry forward” with the person it came from, if you can; it can be a meaningful conversation. Keep your “do differently” list as a gentle guide, not a test. Bonding with your baby may happen quickly or grow over weeks and months; both are normal.

Reflecting on how you were mothered can bring up painful memories, especially if your childhood involved neglect, harshness or abuse. Go slowly, and stop if you need to. If memories feel overwhelming or keep coming back, talking with a counsellor or psychologist can help you make peace with the past and feel more confident about the future.

refs: Stern, D. N. (1995). The motherhood constellation: A unified view of parent-infant psychotherapy. Basic Books.

Fraiberg, S., Adelson, E., & Shapiro, V. (1975). Ghosts in the nursery: A psychoanalytic approach to the problems of impaired infant-mother relationships. Journal of the American Academy of Child Psychiatry, 14(3), 387–421.

Lieberman, A. F., Padrón, E., Van Horn, P., & Harris, W. W. (2005). Angels in the nursery: The intergenerational transmission of benevolent parental influences. Infant Mental Health Journal, 26(6), 504–520.
